facts.label: Source-quality and version relationships
facts.text: - Three 10-Qs, three releases and one 10-K are distinct documents for distinct periods. No source is a duplicate of another; none is draft; all are filed or furnished and unaudited except the 10-K. - Overlap: each release repeats statements that the matching 10-Q also files. Downstream modules must state which basis they use. - Basis difference to carry forward: the release adjusted free cash flow uses capital expenditures net of proceeds from asset sales, while the cash flow statement lists capital expenditures and asset sale proceeds on separate lines. - Conflict between 10-K sections: the debt note describes the exchangeable notes as due June 2029 (10-K page:103), while the exhibit index describes the indenture as for 1.750% Senior Exchangeable Notes "due 2027" (10-K page:135). facts.label: CP-1 (canonical financial data)
facts.text: Evidence: the debt note lists each series with its balance (September 2026 report page:15), the credit agreement has dated terms, a covenant ratio is reported each quarter end (E3, E19, E20, E17), and letter-of-credit facility availability is tabulated (E4). Risk mechanism: the maturity table by year exists only as of year-end 2025 (E15), before the January 2026 redemption of the 7.50% notes (10-K page:103) and the redemption of part of the 9.125% notes (E9; the October release places it in the third quarter), so a maturity wall copied from it would misstate refinancing timing. FY2025 consolidated adjusted EBITDA is not printed under that name in the annual report, which limits a like-for-like LTM build to the release period columns and the segment note, and the adjusted EBITDA definition is the issuer's own (E23). Consequence: CP-1 can run, must rebuild the maturity profile from the instrument list, must state the debt basis it uses (principal versus carrying value), and must label cash interest as FY2025 only. Verdict: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS.

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: On the filed evidence, Nabors Industries Ltd entered 2026 with 2,529.1 US$m of notes at face value and ended Q3 2026 with 2,050.0, after redeeming the 7.50% notes due January 2028 and 100.0 US$m of the 9.125% notes due January 2030 with cash on hand. Because both redemptions were paid from cash, which fell from 940.7 to 475.1 US$m, net debt on a face-value basis moved only from 1,588.4 to 1,574.9 US$m, and net leverage on LTM adjusted EBITDA moved from 1.74x to 1.76x while gross leverage fell from 2.77x to 2.29x. Liquidity, cash plus the undrawn 350.0 US$m revolver, fell from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m, which remains sizeable against a first maturity in June 2029 but is a smaller cushion than at December 31, 2025. The reported covenant interest coverage ratio was 5.20x at September 30, 2026 against a minimum of 2.75x, and minimum guarantor value was 99.8% against 90%. Three features limit how far these figures can be pushed: consolidated cash, debt capacity and EBITDA include the 50%-owned SANAD venture; 2026 cash interest and the covenant EBITDA definition are not in the pack; and the FY2025 comparison includes Quail Tools. All figures below are issuer-reported or calculated from reported inputs, with the formula in Calculations.

facts.label: Definition review
facts.text: - Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted operating income are issuer non-GAAP measures that exclude investment income, interest, gains on the Quail Tools sale and bargain purchase, and Other, net, and the issuer states that they exclude "certain cash expenses that the Company is obligated to make" (ER Q3 page:7). In 9M 2026 Other, net included severance and reorganization costs of 6,203 and litigation items of (14,737), a net credit (10-Q Q3 page:24). The measure includes 100% of the consolidated SANAD venture although Saudi Aramco owns half; net income attributable to noncontrolling interest was 67,384 in 9M 2026 against consolidated net income of 18,723. - The covenant EBITDA in the 2024 Credit Agreement is a defined term not reproduced in the pack. The reported covenant ratio (5.20x) is above this handoff's adjusted EBITDA over interest expense (4.99x); the difference cannot be explained from the pack. - Net debt: the issuer deducts cash and short-term investments from total debt after deferred financing costs. This handoff uses face value for leverage and reports the issuer measure alongside it; the gap at September 30, 2026 equals the deferred financing costs of 27,242. - Adjusted free cash flow: operating cash flow less capital expenditures net of proceeds from sales of assets, before acquisition-related costs (ER Q3 page:12). The cash flow statement shows capital expenditures and sales proceeds on separate lines. - Restricted cash of 2,379 at September 30, 2026 is not in cash and short-term investments (10-Q Q3 page:5). - Secured versus unsecured: the credit agreement is secured by a first lien on contiguous U.S. land drilling rigs (10-K page:30). The pack does not state the security or ranking of any note series beyond the names "senior priority guaranteed" and "senior guaranteed" and the existence of guarantees. No secured or unsecured split of notes is made.

facts.label: Narrative findings
facts.text: Leverage. Evidence: notes at face value fell from 2,529.1 to 2,050.0 US$m while LTM adjusted EBITDA is 893.6 US$m (Financials and credit metrics). Risk mechanism: the reduction was paid from cash, not from free cash flow, because operating cash flow less net capital expenditures was only 38.6 US$m in 9M 2026; net debt on face value is little changed, so the improvement in gross leverage does not add equal protection for creditors. Credit implication: gross leverage of 2.29x overstates the deleveraging; net leverage of 1.76x is the better reference and is flat to FY2025. Because FY2025 EBITDA includes at least 57.3 US$m from Quail Tools (Q2 2025 37.0 plus Q3 2025 20.3, calculated; Q1 2025 stub not supplied) which was sold in August 2025, the LTM figure is the cleaner earnings base.

facts.text: Cash flow quality. Evidence: operating cash flow of 487.5 US$m in 9M 2026 against 448.8 US$m of net capital expenditures; working capital used 48.3 US$m (10-Q Q3 page:43); receivables rose to 511.7 US$m from 391.7 US$m, including related party receivables up to 211.5 US$m, a group that the 10-K says includes the joint venture partner Saudi Aramco (10-K page:114). Risk mechanism: growth in related party receivables and the Mexican late-payment history tie cash conversion to few counterparties, and the rise in receivables sold from 137.0 to 168.0 US$m, a calculated 31.0 US$m, supported operating cash flow in the nine months because sale proceeds are classified as operating (10-Q Q3 page:14). facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: On the filed evidence, Nabors Industries Ltd is an operating drilling contractor and not a sponsor-owned or recently recapitalised credit: no financial sponsor, controlling holder or dividend recapitalisation appears in the pack, and the transactions of the last two years are an equity-funded acquisition (Parker, closed March 11, 2025), a cash sale of the acquired Quail Tools business (August 20, 2025), a bond refinancing (November 10, 2025) and cash-funded note redemptions through Q3 2026. The business risk that matters most to a creditor is concentration: Saudi Aramco is both the largest customer, about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues, and the 50% partner in the consolidated SANAD joint venture, so revenue visibility, receivables, capital spending and a call option on Nabors' own interest all run through one relationship. The operating model is daywork contracting for rigs plus technology and equipment segments, with pricing set by dayrate and volume by rigs working; the filings do not quantify contract backlog or SANAD's own earnings, and the October release states a suspension of five SANAD rigs that the filed quarterly report does not. Governance behaviour is documented through related-party notes and the credit agreement's restricted payment terms rather than through any distribution or priming action; no behaviour in the Extraction-Oriented or Creditor-Adverse categories is evidenced, and ownership percentages cannot be stated because they sit in the proxy statement, which is not in the pack.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Parker Drilling Company was acquired on March 11, 2025 as a wholly owned subsidiary for consideration of 4.8 million Nabors common shares plus a small cash payment, valued at about 180.6 US$m at the closing share price; the status is closed and the accounting is the acquisition method, with a bargain purchase gain recorded because the share price fell between signing on October 14, 2024 and closing (10-Q Q3 page:9; E11). No debt was raised for the purchase, but Parker's 13% second lien term loan of 177.8 US$m, which carried a change of control repayment trigger, was repaid on March 25, 2025 using the 2024 Credit Agreement (10-K page:105); revolver borrowings of 398.0 US$m in 2025 were fully repaid in 2025 (10-K page:83) and the revolver was undrawn at December 31, 2025, so the acquisition added no permanent secured debt on the filed evidence. Quail Tools, part of the Parker acquisition, was sold to Superior Energy Services, Inc. on August 20, 2025; the 10-K gives net consideration as 625.0 US$m including a working capital adjustment, and the 10-Q gives it as 600.0 US$m plus working capital adjustments, with cash of 375.0 US$m and a seller note of 250.0 US$m in both; the seller note was prepaid in full on October 9, 2025 (E12, E13). That difference is logged as a conflict below and is not reconciled.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: On new debt, Nabors issued 700.0 US$m of 7.625% senior priority guaranteed notes due November 2032 on November 10, 2025 and used the net proceeds to redeem all of its 7.375% senior priority guaranteed notes due May 2027, of which 546.1 US$m remained, for about 557.1 US$m in cash including a 10.1 US$m premium (10-K page:104 and page:59). Earlier issues still outstanding are the 1.75% senior exchangeable notes of 250.0 US$m (February 2023), the 9.125% notes, 650.0 US$m outstanding at December 31, 2025 (indenture dated November 20, 2023), and the 8.875% notes of 550.0 US$m (indenture dated July 22, 2024) (10-K page:103 to page:104 and page:135). No new debt was issued in 2026 through the cutoff: the 7.50% senior guaranteed notes due January 2028 were redeemed on January 15, 2026, and 100.0 US$m of the 9.125% notes was redeemed for about 104.9 US$m in cash in the third quarter, taking notes at face value to 2,050.0 US$m (10-K page:103; 10-Q Q3 page:15; CP-1). On April 7, 2026 a joinder increased the credit agreement's letter of credit tranche by 25.0 US$m, and on September 4, 2025 the first amendment let Nabors Delaware repurchase up to 100.0 US$m of equity a year, reducing dividend capacity dollar for dollar (10-Q Q3 page:16). The special purpose acquisition company NETC II, co-sponsored with an entity owned by members of management and directors, failed to complete its planned combination with e2Companies; after litigation, a settlement on October 14, 2025 gave NETC II a secured promissory note from e2 of 29.23 US$m, and 10.6 US$m of settlement income was recorded in Other, net in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:30; 10-K page:113).

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: Revenue durability and concentration. Evidence: Saudi Aramco about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues, the three largest customers about 41%, contracts per rig through SANAD (E4, E5, E22), and 2026 suspension and reactivation notices in the Middle East (E24, E32). Risk mechanic: per-rig contracts let a customer idle rigs without a contract termination, so a suspension reduces revenue, EBITDA and receivable inflows at once while SANAD's newbuild obligations and Nabors' backstop continue; 41% of receivables sit in Saudi Arabia. Credit implication: debt service capacity depends on one counterparty's rig program, so the monitoring posture should track SANAD rig count and receivables from Saudi Arabia each quarter; the Q3 2026 filed rig counts rose, but management reports five suspended rigs after quarter end. Countering logged item: conflict C3 (Aramco share versus related-party revenue) means the size of the concentration is not fully pinned down.

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: daywork dayrate contracts, lower U.S. dayrates offset by volume, improving international pricing, and a management guide that includes a large SANAD newbuild program (E19, E23, E24, E27). Risk mechanic: margin depends on dayrate and rigs working, while SANAD capital spending is front-loaded and its timing has shifted to later periods. Credit implication: free cash flow after capital spending is sensitive to SANAD milestone timing, so the debt reduction already achieved came from cash balances rather than recurring surplus (CP-1).

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: The fundamental credit view of Nabors Industries Ltd as of 2026-11-05 is balanced, with financial risk moderate and business risk elevated, and the confidence is Medium because the evidence is complete enough to judge direction but several datapoints that would move the view are missing. On the financial side, notes at face value stand at 2,050.0 US$m, net debt is 1,574.9 US$m or 1.76x LTM adjusted EBITDA of 893.6 US$m, gross leverage is 2.29x, no note matures before the 250.0 US$m exchangeable notes in June 2029, the revolver is undrawn at 350.0 US$m, and the reported covenant interest coverage of 5.20x sits well above the 2.75x minimum. The weakening features are the use of cash to fund the deleveraging, which lowered liquidity from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m while net leverage stayed flat at 1.74x to 1.76x, and a free cash flow margin over fixed charges that is thin. On the business side, Saudi Aramco is about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues and the 50% partner in the consolidated SANAD venture, so revenue durability, receivables, a large newbuild capital program and a change-of-control call option all depend on one relationship; the filings show reactivations of Saudi rigs during 2026 and the October release reports five suspended SANAD rigs, which are management statements not yet in a filing. Governance evidence is neutral to supportive: debt has been repaid in cash, no sponsor or creditor-adverse action is documented, and the related-party arrangements are disclosed but only partly quantified. What would change the view: confirmed Saudi suspensions that cut earnings or collections, a non-renewal of the receivables facility, or evidence that SANAD cash and earnings are less accessible to creditors than the consolidated figures imply would weaken it; sustained free cash flow above fixed charges and further cash-funded debt reduction without eroding liquidity would strengthen it.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The most important finding is concentration: Saudi Aramco accounted for about 30% of FY2025 consolidated operating revenues, the three largest contract drilling customers for about 41%, and about 41% of net receivables at September 30, 2026 were in Saudi Arabia. Because Aramco contracts are per rig and mainly run through SANAD, a customer decision to idle rigs cuts revenue and earnings without any contract termination, and the October release reports five suspended SANAD rigs against a quarter in which rig counts rose. That statement is management's, and until a filing confirms it the size of the effect cannot be stated.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The second finding is that leverage is moderate and has fallen on a gross basis only. Notes at face value fell from 2,529.1 to 2,050.0 US$m, gross leverage from 2.77x to 2.29x, but net debt moved only from 1,588.4 to 1,574.9 US$m, because the redemptions of the 2028 notes and part of the 2030 notes were paid from cash that fell from 940.7 to 475.1 US$m. Liquidity of cash plus the undrawn revolver therefore fell from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m. Third, the maturity profile is long: nothing matures before 250.0 US$m in June 2029, followed by 550.0, 550.0 and 700.0 US$m in 2030, 2031 and 2032, and the revolver runs to the earlier of June 17, 2029 and a springing date tied to the exchangeable notes; this limits refinancing risk for several years but concentrates 1,800.0 US$m in 2030 to 2032.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. Moderate leverage with a long runway: net leverage of 1.76x on face value, the first maturity in June 2029, and a revolver that is undrawn and matures no earlier than that date. Reported covenant headroom is wide, with interest coverage at 5.20x against 2.75x and minimum guarantor value at 99.8% against 90%, though the covenant definition is not available to test. Diversification across four segments and across the U.S. and international drilling, with technology and equipment segments that sell to third parties. A demonstrated willingness to repay debt in cash and to refinance ahead of maturity, shown by the 2025 refinancing and the 2026 redemptions. Adjusted EBITDA on an LTM basis is above 890 US$m with interest cover on interest expense of 4.99x and falling coupons.

facts.text: Weaknesses. Heavy dependence on issuer-defined adjusted EBITDA that excludes certain cash expenses and includes all of SANAD. Information gaps on guarantors, ranking, covenant definitions, backlog and ownership. History distorted by gains and disposals in FY2025.

### Source-by-source assessment
#### Annual report, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 (10-K)

- Authority and perimeter: original filed audited annual report of Nabors Industries Ltd. and subsidiaries, consolidated. Items 1 to 16 and Notes 1 to 20 are present (Item 1 at page:4, Item 7 at page:57, Item 8 at page:75, Note 9 Debt at page:103, Note 12 Joint Ventures at page:111, Note 17 Segment Information at page:121, Note 19 Leases at page:126). This is the only audited source and the only source with a lease note, full-year supplemental cash flow information and a statement of exhibits.

- Coverage: debt by instrument and a principal maturity table as of December 31, 2025 (page:103); the covenant statement as of year-end (page:63); first-lien security description (page:30); lease position (page:127); cash paid for interest and income taxes for 2025, 2024 and 2023 (page:121).

- Limits: the text does not print a consolidated line named Adjusted EBITDA; the segment note prints total adjusted operating income and depreciation and amortization (page:122). No rating-agency ratings are printed. The exhibit index lists but does not contain the indentures and credit agreement (pages:135-136).
#### Quarterly reports on Form 10-Q (March 31, June 30 and September 30, 2026)

- Authority and perimeter: original filed unaudited interim reports on a consolidated basis, each prepared under interim reporting rules (the September report says it is to be read together with the 2025 annual report). They are separate, successive documents; none supersedes another. The September 30, 2026 report is the latest and carries the balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement (nine months only), notes and management discussion.

- Coverage: the debt note by instrument (September 30 report page:15, March 31 report page:13, June 30 report page:13), the credit agreement terms and Joinder (page:15 to page:16 of the September report), covenant ratios at each quarter end (March 31 page:33, June 30 page:37, September 30 page:40), letter-of-credit facility availability (page:40 to page:41), the receivables purchase and sales agreements (page:14, page:41), purchase commitments (page:42), joint venture balance sheet (page:13) and segment information (page:24).

- Limits: cash flow statements are year-to-date, so discrete quarters other than the first need the releases or subtraction downstream; no lease note, no debt maturity table by year, and no cash paid for interest or income taxes were found in the three reports after a search for those terms and their variants (the only matches were an accounting-standard paragraph and investing-activity lines); no separate subsequent events note was found.
#### Earnings releases, Exhibit 99.1 (April 28, July 28 and October 27, 2026)
- Authority: issuer press releases furnished with Form 8-K; management attributed claims and non-GAAP measures with reconciliations. They do not override the filed reports.

- Coverage: adjusted EBITDA, adjusted operating income and adjusted free cash flow with reconciliations to net income and to operating cash flow (October release page:9 to page:12); net debt reconciliation (page:11 of each release); segment results and rig activity (October release page:6 to page:7); outlook and guidance (October release page:3 to page:4); condensed income statement and balance sheet (page:5 to page:6).

- Limits: the releases are unaudited, the guidance cannot be reconciled by the issuer ("We do not provide a forward-looking reconciliation"), and the October release presents a Quail Tools carve-out for the prior-year quarter only. - Basis difference to carry forward: the release net debt reconciliation takes total debt after deferred financing costs, while the debt note also lists principal amounts before those costs. Downstream modules must state which basis they use.

- Basis difference to carry forward: the release adjusted free cash flow uses capital expenditures net of proceeds from asset sales, while the cash flow statement lists capital expenditures and asset sale proceeds on separate lines.

- Conflict between 10-K sections: the debt note describes the exchangeable notes as due June 2029 (10-K page:103), while the exhibit index describes the indenture as for 1.750% Senior Exchangeable Notes "due 2027" (10-K page:135). ### Consumer assessments
#### CP-1 (canonical financial data)

Evidence: the debt note lists each series with its balance (September 2026 report page:15), the credit agreement has dated terms, a covenant ratio is reported each quarter end (E3, E19, E20, E17), and letter-of-credit facility availability is tabulated (E4). Risk mechanism: the maturity table by year exists only as of year-end 2025 (E15), before the January 2026 redemption of the 7.50% notes (10-K page:103) and the redemption of part of the 9.125% notes (E9; the October release places it in the third quarter), so a maturity wall copied from it would misstate refinancing timing. FY2025 consolidated adjusted EBITDA is not printed under that name in the annual report, which limits a like-for-like LTM build to the release period columns and the segment note, and the adjusted EBITDA definition is the issuer's own (E23). Consequence: CP-1 can run, must rebuild the maturity profile from the instrument list, must state the debt basis it uses (principal versus carrying value), and must label cash interest as FY2025 only. Verdict: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS.
#### CP-1A (business and transaction context)

Evidence: Item 1 of the annual report, Notes 3 and 4 of the 10-Qs, and three releases describe the Parker acquisition, the Quail Tools sale (E24), SANAD (E6) and segment structure. Risk mechanism: only filing descriptions exist for these transactions, with no executed merger or sale agreements, so deal terms and any creditor-relevant covenants of those documents cannot be checked; the release statement on rig suspensions (E21) is management language and the 10-Q only speaks of suspension notices in general (E11). Governance and ownership detail is limited to what the filings state; no sponsor exists in context. Consequence: CP-1A can run and must tag management statements as such. Verdict: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS.
#### CP-2 (fundamental credit synthesis)

Evidence: CP-2 consumes only upstream CP-1 and CP-1A registers, so its source need is the sum of theirs. Risk mechanism: the absence of ratings in context and sources beyond a statement of past downgrade to non-investment grade (E12), of peer data and of executed legal terms narrows what it can say on recovery and relative position. Consequence: CP-2 can run if CP-1 and CP-1A are settled; the dependency planner orders it, and its gaps ledger should carry the items below. Verdict: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS.
#### CP-5 (evidence trace validator)

Evidence: all quotes and figures can be matched to seven pinned filings, and the same fact appears in both a release and a 10-Q for each quarter. Risk mechanism: the overlap is where cross-module identity can fail (principal versus carrying debt; gross versus net capital expenditures; the 2027 versus 2029 exchangeable-note wording at E14). Consequence: CP-5 can run; it should treat the 10-Q as controlling over the release and flag basis differences instead of treating them as errors. Verdict: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS.
### Reasoning chain for the main limitation

Evidence: the exhibit index lists indentures, with guarantors named only for one 2020 indenture (E28) and as "the guarantors party thereto" for the others (E29). Source risk mechanism: the guarantor set of the priority guaranteed notes, which the debt note calls "certain of Nabors’ indirect wholly-owned subsidiaries" (E16), and the covenant definitions behind the reported ratio (E3) are not readable from primary documents, so structural ranking and covenant headroom depend on management summaries. Downstream consequence: CP-1 can report the reported ratio and its stated minimum, but cannot recompute the covenant definition of EBITDA, and CP-2 must hold structural-priority conclusions as limited.
## Calculations
No financial figure was calculated, normalized or reconciled in this module, as the method requires. The only counts are page counts of the retained extractions, taken from the pack:
| Item | Inputs | Result |
| Pages retained across the seven issuer sources | 143 + 40 + 44 + 46 + 11 + 12 + 12 | 308 of 308 pages present in the extraction |
| Quarterly reports present | March 31, 2026; June 30, 2026; September 30, 2026 | 3 of 3 expected for the latest three quarters |
| Earnings releases present | April 28, 2026; July 28, 2026; October 27, 2026 | 3 of 3 expected for the latest three quarters |

Retained means present in the extraction; it does not mean each page was individually read for this module. Pages read for this review were the cover, statements, debt, joint venture, receivables, liquidity, covenant, commitments, segment and exhibit-index pages cited above, the full October release, and the main parts of each other source named in the assessment.
## Gaps

| G1 | Executed indentures and the 2024 Credit Agreement are not in the pack (the context sets legal documents to none); guarantor names, covenant definitions and call terms rest on filing summaries | Medium | CP-1, CP-2, CP-5 | Add the indentures and credit agreement from the exhibit index if a legal-structure review is required |
| G2 | No rating-agency report or rating in context; the filings only state a past downgrade to non-investment grade | Medium | CP-2 | Supply current ratings if a rating view is needed |
| G3 | The year-by-year debt maturity table is printed only as of December 31, 2025; no later table found | Medium | CP-1 | Rebuild from the instrument list in the debt note |

| G4 | Cash paid for interest and income taxes is printed for FY2025 only; not found in the three 10-Qs after searching "paid for", "interest paid", "taxes paid" and "supplemental cash" | Medium | CP-1 | Use FY2025 figure labelled as such; interest expense is a different measure |

| G5 | The 10-K does not print consolidated Adjusted EBITDA by name; FY2025 consolidated adjusted EBITDA needs the segment note or release columns; no fourth-quarter 2025 release is in the pack | Medium | CP-1 | Use the release columns and label the basis; request the fourth-quarter 2025 release if needed |
| G6 | The covenant EBITDA definition is not in the pack; the reported ratio cannot be recomputed | Medium | CP-1, CP-2 | Add the credit agreement |

| G7 | Exhibit index wording "due 2027" conflicts with the debt note "due June 2029" for the exchangeable notes | Low | CP-1, CP-5 | Treat the debt note as controlling; confirm in the indenture if added |
| G8 | Release-only statements (five Saudi rig suspensions, guidance, run-rate claims) are not in the filed 10-Q | Low | CP-1A, CP-2, CP-5 | Carry as management language |
| G9 | No executed Parker merger or Quail Tools sale agreement | Low | CP-1A | Not needed for a snapshot; add for transaction review |

| G11 | Parent, sponsor, restricted group and guarantor designations are blank in context | Low | CP-1A, CP-2 | Leave as not supplied |
| G12 | Part of the 10-K (risk factors and governance items) was not read page by page in this module | Low | CP-1A | CP-1A reads the pages it needs |
## Next module

The next module is CP-1, which can run on the retained sources. It should start with the September 30, 2026 quarterly report and the October 27, 2026 release, label every figure Q3 2026, nine months 2026 or FY2025, rebuild the maturity profile from the instrument list rather than the year-end 2025 table, state the debt basis it uses, treat cash interest as FY2025 only, and carry G1 to G7 forward. CP-1A, CP-2 and CP-5 follow in the planner's order, and each should carry these limitations. Command sheet: CP-1 RUN, CP-1A RUN, CP-2 RUN, CP-5 RUN; no consumer is DO NOT RUN.

### Financial base view

On the filed evidence, Nabors Industries Ltd entered 2026 with 2,529.1 US$m of notes at face value and ended Q3 2026 with 2,050.0, after redeeming the 7.50% notes due January 2028 and 100.0 US$m of the 9.125% notes due January 2030 with cash on hand. Because both redemptions were paid from cash, which fell from 940.7 to 475.1 US$m, net debt on a face-value basis moved only from 1,588.4 to 1,574.9 US$m, and net leverage on LTM adjusted EBITDA moved from 1.74x to 1.76x while gross leverage fell from 2.77x to 2.29x. Liquidity, cash plus the undrawn 350.0 US$m revolver, fell from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m, which remains sizeable against a first maturity in June 2029 but is a smaller cushion than at December 31, 2025. The reported covenant interest coverage ratio was 5.20x at September 30, 2026 against a minimum of 2.75x, and minimum guarantor value was 99.8% against 90%. Three features limit how far these figures can be pushed: consolidated cash, debt capacity and EBITDA include the 50%-owned SANAD venture; 2026 cash interest and the covenant EBITDA definition are not in the pack; and the FY2025 comparison includes Quail Tools. All figures below are issuer-reported or calculated from reported inputs, with the formula in Calculations.

### Definition review

- Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted operating income are issuer non-GAAP measures that exclude investment income, interest, gains on the Quail Tools sale and bargain purchase, and Other, net, and the issuer states that they exclude "certain cash expenses that the Company is obligated to make" (ER Q3 page:7). In 9M 2026 Other, net included severance and reorganization costs of 6,203 and litigation items of (14,737), a net credit (10-Q Q3 page:24). The measure includes 100% of the consolidated SANAD venture although Saudi Aramco owns half; net income attributable to noncontrolling interest was 67,384 in 9M 2026 against consolidated net income of 18,723.

- The covenant EBITDA in the 2024 Credit Agreement is a defined term not reproduced in the pack. The reported covenant ratio (5.20x) is above this handoff's adjusted EBITDA over interest expense (4.99x); the difference cannot be explained from the pack.

- Net debt: the issuer deducts cash and short-term investments from total debt after deferred financing costs. This handoff uses face value for leverage and reports the issuer measure alongside it; the gap at September 30, 2026 equals the deferred financing costs of 27,242.

- Adjusted free cash flow: operating cash flow less capital expenditures net of proceeds from sales of assets, before acquisition-related costs (ER Q3 page:12). The cash flow statement shows capital expenditures and sales proceeds on separate lines.
- Restricted cash of 2,379 at September 30, 2026 is not in cash and short-term investments (10-Q Q3 page:5).

- Secured versus unsecured: the credit agreement is secured by a first lien on contiguous U.S. land drilling rigs (10-K page:30). The pack does not state the security or ranking of any note series beyond the names "senior priority guaranteed" and "senior guaranteed" and the existence of guarantees. No secured or unsecured split of notes is made.
### Funding, off-debt claims and commitments

- Redeemable noncontrolling interest, 502,718 at September 30, 2026: Saudi Aramco's share of SANAD redeemable ownership interests, which accrue interest annually, have a twenty-five year maturity and convert to authorized capital on specified events including accumulated losses (10-Q Q3 page:13). It is mezzanine equity, outside debt, and the accrued distribution of 20,272 for 9M 2026 reduced retained earnings (10-Q Q3 page:6).

- SANAD: balance sheet at September 30, 2026 shows cash of 180,635, total assets of 1,570,831 and total liabilities of 244,920 (10-Q Q3 page:13). The 10-K states that Nabors backstops its share of SANAD's obligations to purchase the first 25 drilling rigs if the venture lacks cash or third-party financing (10-K page:114); the Q3 10-Q does not repeat that sentence in the pages searched.

- Receivables sale: 168,000 sold and uncollected at September 30, 2026, against 138,000 at June 30, 2026 and 137,000 at December 31, 2025 (10-Q Q3 page:15; 10-Q Q2 page:13); outside reported debt under sale accounting; the originators, Nabors Industries, Inc., the special purpose entity and the Company give representations, covenants and an indemnification guarantee (10-Q Q3 page:41).
- Purchase commitments of about 296.4 US$m at September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:42). Financial standby letters of credit and surety instruments of 33,795 maximum (10-Q Q3 page:44).

- Leases: operating lease liabilities of 40,213 at December 31, 2025 (10-K page:127); the September 30, 2026 balance sheet shows current lease liabilities of 10,206 (10-Q Q3 page:2). No finance leases and no pension funded status were located.

- Related parties: revenues from related parties including Saudi Aramco were about 1.1 billion US$ in FY2025 (10-K page:114), and related party receivables were 211.5 US$m at September 30, 2026 against 121.0 at December 31, 2025 (10-Q Q3 page:3).
- Receivables concentration at September 30, 2026: about 41% Saudi Arabia, 13% U.S. and 9% Mexico, with a Mexican customer that has a history of late payment (10-Q Q3 page:41).
### Latest quarter and events after the quarter end

- Q3 2026 financing: 100.0 US$m of the 9.125% notes redeemed with cash (10-Q Q3 page:15; ER Q3 page:3); loss on debt buybacks of 5,525 in Q3 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:24). April 7, 2026: the letter of credit tranche was increased by 25.0 US$m (10-Q Q3 page:16). On August 26, 2026, Nabors issued about 0.4 million shares for about 5.4 million Series B-1 preferred shares of Quaise Energy, a noncash exchange valued by reference to 35.0 US$m (10-Q Q3 page:17).

- After September 30, 2026 and up to the cutoff: the October 27, 2026 release states that SANAD has suspended five rigs and gives fourth-quarter guidance (ER Q3 page:2 and page:3-4); management expects full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about 930 US$m, adjusted free cash flow of 100 to 110 US$m and capital spending of 710 to 720 US$m, including 295 to 305 for SANAD newbuilds. These are management statements; the filed 10-Q does not give the rig suspension count. No debt issuance, redemption or amendment dated after September 30, 2026 appears in the pack.
- The Q3 10-Q also notes that, in the Middle East, certain operators have placed rigs on standby and issued additional suspension notices (10-Q Q3 page:33).
### Narrative findings

**Leverage.** Evidence: notes at face value fell from 2,529.1 to 2,050.0 US$m while LTM adjusted EBITDA is 893.6 US$m (Financials and credit metrics). Risk mechanism: the reduction was paid from cash, not from free cash flow, because operating cash flow less net capital expenditures was only 38.6 US$m in 9M 2026; net debt on face value is little changed, so the improvement in gross leverage does not add equal protection for creditors. Credit implication: gross leverage of 2.29x overstates the deleveraging; net leverage of 1.76x is the better reference and is flat to FY2025. Because FY2025 EBITDA includes at least 57.3 US$m from Quail Tools (Q2 2025 37.0 plus Q3 2025 20.3, calculated; Q1 2025 stub not supplied) which was sold in August 2025, the LTM figure is the cleaner earnings base.

**Coverage.** Evidence: interest expense fell from 215.4 to an LTM 179.2 US$m, and annual coupons on notes outstanding are 156.8 US$m against 194.3 US$m on the December 31, 2025 mix. Risk mechanism: coupons on the remaining notes are fixed, so interest expense should fall further toward the coupon run rate, while 2026 cash interest is not reported and the Q3 release says higher cash interest payments partly offset the sequential improvement in free cash flow (F15). Credit implication: cover on interest expense of 4.99x LTM is adequate and improving, and the reported covenant ratio of 5.20x is well above 2.75x, but the covenant definition cannot be tested from the pack.

**Cash flow quality.** Evidence: operating cash flow of 487.5 US$m in 9M 2026 against 448.8 US$m of net capital expenditures; working capital used 48.3 US$m (10-Q Q3 page:43); receivables rose to 511.7 US$m from 391.7 US$m, including related party receivables up to 211.5 US$m, a group that the 10-K says includes the joint venture partner Saudi Aramco (10-K page:114). Risk mechanism: growth in related party receivables and the Mexican late-payment history tie cash conversion to few counterparties, and the rise in receivables sold from 137.0 to 168.0 US$m, a calculated 31.0 US$m, supported operating cash flow in the nine months because sale proceeds are classified as operating (10-Q Q3 page:14). Credit implication: Q3 free cash flow of 74.5 US$m benefited from lower SANAD capital spending as milestones shifted to later periods (ER Q3 page:2 and page:3), so the full-year guidance of 100 to 110 US$m depends on Q4 delivery of 60 to 70 US$m.

**Liquidity.** Evidence: cash and short-term investments of 475.1 US$m and an undrawn 350.0 US$m revolver give 825.1 US$m, down from 1,290.7 US$m. Risk mechanism: 180.6 US$m of the cash sits in SANAD, whose assets can be used to settle the venture's own obligations or be made available to its owners through dividends, distributions or an exchange of redeemable interests upon mutual agreement of the owners (10-Q Q3 page:13), and the receivables facility term may end on April 1, 2027 at the earliest. Credit implication: liquidity outside SANAD is lower than the headline; with no maturity before June 2029 and no borrowings, the near-term refinancing risk is low, but the cushion for a receivables facility non-renewal or an extended Saudi slowdown is thinner than at FY2025.

**Data quality and definition risk.** Evidence: see Definition review. Risk mechanism: issuer-defined EBITDA excludes cash items and includes all of SANAD; the covenant EBITDA is undefined here. Credit implication: use LTM adjusted EBITDA as an issuer-defined base, not as a covenant-equivalent figure.

## Calculations
All inputs are US$ thousands as reported unless stated; results are rounded for the tables. Sign convention: gains reduce the cost-side lines.

| FY2025 adjusted operating income | Income before income taxes 537,528 + interest expense 215,366 - investment income 27,648 - gain on Quail Tools 413,962 - gain on bargain purchase 113,653 + Other, net 65,802 (10-K page:82, with the issuer's stated definition in ER Q3 page:11) | 263,433 |
| FY2025 adjusted EBITDA | 263,433 + depreciation and amortization 649,234 | 912,667 |

### Leverage
| Period | Debt at face value | Cash and short-term investments | Net debt at face value | EBITDA used | Total debt / EBITDA | Net debt / EBITDA |

Sensitivities, not headline figures: adding receivables sold of 168,000 to face-value debt gives (2,050,000 + 168,000) / 893,571 = 2.48x; excluding SANAD cash of 180,635 from cash gives net debt of 2,050,000 - (475,145 - 180,635) = 1,755,490, or 1.96x on the same EBITDA, which still includes 100% of SANAD and so is an overstatement of leverage on a proportionate view and an understatement on a ring-fenced view.

The revolver and letter-of-credit facilities run to June 2029 at the earliest, so none expires within twelve months; the receivables facility may end April 1, 2027, which is within twelve months of the cutoff.

## Gaps
| ID | Gap | Why it matters | Action |

| H1 | Not supplied: cash paid for interest and cash taxes for 2026 periods; the 10-Qs do not print them | Cash interest cover cannot be shown for Q1 to Q3 2026 or LTM; the indicative figure is an inference | Use FY2025 cash interest; ask for the supplemental cash flow data if cash cover is needed |

| H2 | Not supplied: the covenant definition of EBITDA and interest expense, the collateral coverage threshold and appraisal result | Headroom in EBITDA terms and collateral cushion cannot be computed | Add the 2024 Credit Agreement |

| H3 | Not supplied: guarantor lists, security and ranking of each note series, and call or put schedules | Structural subordination and recovery work cannot rely on filings alone | Add the indentures listed in the 10-K exhibit index |

| H4 | The year-by-year maturity table in the 10-K is as of December 31, 2025; a schedule for September 30, 2026 was rebuilt from the instrument list | Face-value schedule only; no amortization or call dates | Treat as the working schedule |

| H5 | SANAD: no income statement, EBITDA or debt capacity of the venture; cash availability to the parent is by distribution or exchange of redeemable interests only | Proportionate leverage and parent-only liquidity cannot be calculated | Request venture-level financial data; run a case that excludes the 180.6 US$m |
| H6 | The backstop of SANAD rig purchases appears in the 10-K but was not found in the Q3 10-Q | Contingent funding exposure after the first 25 rigs is unquantified | Confirm in a later filing |

| H7 | Management statements in the October release (rig suspensions, guidance, run rate) are not repeated in a filing | Not filed evidence; guidance cannot be reconciled by the issuer | Carry as management language |
| H8 | The 10-K does not print consolidated adjusted EBITDA; FY2025 is calculated and checked two ways | Small risk of definitional difference | Both methods agree at 912,667 |

| H9 | Receivables facility: availability, concentration limits and the effect on operating cash flow are not quantified | Non-renewal after April 1, 2027 would absorb cash | Monitor the term and the amount sold |
| H10 | No ratings, quotes, market capitalization or peer data in the pack | Market-based leverage and relative value are outside this base | Not supplied in context |

| H11 | Pension funded status and finance leases were not located; operating lease liability only as of December 31, 2025 | Small, but leases and pensions are outside the debt figure | Confirm in the 10-K notes if needed |
| H12 | Exhibit-index wording "due 2027" for the exchangeable notes conflicts with the debt note "due June 2029" | Maturity label only | The debt note and the quarterly tables control |
## Next module

Next is CP-1A (business and transaction context), which should use this handoff for the Parker acquisition and Quail Tools sale dates, the SANAD joint venture mechanics and the Saudi concentration, and carry H3, H5, H6 and H7. CP-2 should take the leverage, coverage, liquidity and cash flow figures above as calculated on the stated bases (face-value debt, issuer-defined LTM adjusted EBITDA) and state that 2026 cash interest and the covenant EBITDA definition are not available. CP-5 should treat the 10-Q as controlling over the release, check the three basis differences (face versus carrying debt, gross versus net capital expenditures, issuer versus covenant EBITDA) as definitional rather than errors, and verify the calculated figures against the inputs listed in Calculations.

- Issuer: NABORS INDUSTRIES LTD (issuer id nbr, NYSE: NBR), the Bermuda holding company that files consolidated statements; Nabors Industries, Inc. ("Nabors Delaware") is the wholly owned borrower under the 2024 Credit Agreement.
- As-of date: 2026-11-05. Evidence cutoff: 2026-11-05. Events after September 30, 2026 are labelled as subsequent events and are not folded into Q3 2026 facts.
- Pathway: credit_snapshot, public case. Reporting currency: USD. Current period Q3 2026; prior period FY2025.

- Task for this module: the business and transaction fact pack a committee reads first, from a creditor perspective: transaction and ownership structure, business and operating model, credit-relevant history and change, issuer-level governance behaviour, credit translations, conflicts and the monitoring gaps. No peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion is given.

- Upstream handoffs used: CP-0 (source readiness) and CP-1 (financial base), both listed in Sources. Figures are quoted from the sources or from CP-1 on the same basis; no CP-1 figure is changed here. CP-1 gap H3 (guarantor lists and ranking), H5 (SANAD venture data), H6 (rig-purchase backstop) and H7 (release-only statements) are carried forward below.

- Category tags used on every fact row: Documentary Fact (the cited source states it), Management Language (management's characterisation, quoted and qualified), Analyst Interpretation (a reading of cited evidence) and Insufficient Information (evidence missing; the missing datapoint and its importance are stated).

- Settings file `context` is user input, not issuer evidence. It lists sector "Drilling Oil & Gas Wells" and country "United States" and leaves sponsor, parent, borrower, guarantors, ratings and deal terms blank; blanks are treated as not supplied, never as none or zero.
- No external material is used. A page locator is the source chunk shown as `page:N`, not a printed page.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Nabors is a listed drilling contractor with no sponsor. Its credit depends on Saudi Aramco, 30% of FY2025 revenue and half-owner of the SANAD venture. Recent transactions reduced debt, and no debt-funded distribution is documented. | Medium | Beneficial ownership, contract backlog and venture-level financials are not in the pack, and management statements on rig suspensions and guidance are not filed evidence. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Saudi Aramco accounted for about 30% of FY2025 revenue and the three largest customers for 41%; Aramco contracts are per rig, mainly through SANAD. | Revenue visibility and cash conversion depend on one counterparty, so rig suspensions there hit earnings and receivables together. | High |

| The October release says SANAD suspended five rigs, after earlier 2026 reactivations; the filed quarterly report mentions suspension notices only in general terms. | Saudi activity can reverse quickly; treat the suspensions as management statements until a filing confirms them. | Medium |

| Parker was acquired for 4.8 million shares, and Quail Tools, acquired with Parker, was sold in August 2025. | Growth was added without new debt and a business was sold for cash, but FY2025 comparisons include earnings no longer owned. | Medium |

| Management-linked related-party arrangements exist: a profit-sharing venture, a SPAC sponsor entity and director-affiliated services. | Where quantified the amounts are small against earnings; unquantified items are leakage channels to monitor, and no creditor-adverse action is documented. | Medium |

### Business and transaction view

On the filed evidence, Nabors Industries Ltd is an operating drilling contractor and not a sponsor-owned or recently recapitalised credit: no financial sponsor, controlling holder or dividend recapitalisation appears in the pack, and the transactions of the last two years are an equity-funded acquisition (Parker, closed March 11, 2025), a cash sale of the acquired Quail Tools business (August 20, 2025), a bond refinancing (November 10, 2025) and cash-funded note redemptions through Q3 2026. The business risk that matters most to a creditor is concentration: Saudi Aramco is both the largest customer, about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues, and the 50% partner in the consolidated SANAD joint venture, so revenue visibility, receivables, capital spending and a call option on Nabors' own interest all run through one relationship. The operating model is daywork contracting for rigs plus technology and equipment segments, with pricing set by dayrate and volume by rigs working; the filings do not quantify contract backlog or SANAD's own earnings, and the October release states a suspension of five SANAD rigs that the filed quarterly report does not. Governance behaviour is documented through related-party notes and the credit agreement's restricted payment terms rather than through any distribution or priming action; no behaviour in the Extraction-Oriented or Creditor-Adverse categories is evidenced, and ownership percentages cannot be stated because they sit in the proxy statement, which is not in the pack.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Parker Drilling Company was acquired on March 11, 2025 as a wholly owned subsidiary for consideration of 4.8 million Nabors common shares plus a small cash payment, valued at about 180.6 US$m at the closing share price; the status is closed and the accounting is the acquisition method, with a bargain purchase gain recorded because the share price fell between signing on October 14, 2024 and closing (10-Q Q3 page:9; E11). No debt was raised for the purchase, but Parker's 13% second lien term loan of 177.8 US$m, which carried a change of control repayment trigger, was repaid on March 25, 2025 using the 2024 Credit Agreement (10-K page:105); revolver borrowings of 398.0 US$m in 2025 were fully repaid in 2025 (10-K page:83) and the revolver was undrawn at December 31, 2025, so the acquisition added no permanent secured debt on the filed evidence. Quail Tools, part of the Parker acquisition, was sold to Superior Energy Services, Inc. on August 20, 2025; the 10-K gives net consideration as 625.0 US$m including a working capital adjustment, and the 10-Q gives it as 600.0 US$m plus working capital adjustments, with cash of 375.0 US$m and a seller note of 250.0 US$m in both; the seller note was prepaid in full on October 9, 2025 (E12, E13). That difference is logged as a conflict below and is not reconciled.

On new debt, Nabors issued 700.0 US$m of 7.625% senior priority guaranteed notes due November 2032 on November 10, 2025 and used the net proceeds to redeem all of its 7.375% senior priority guaranteed notes due May 2027, of which 546.1 US$m remained, for about 557.1 US$m in cash including a 10.1 US$m premium (10-K page:104 and page:59). Earlier issues still outstanding are the 1.75% senior exchangeable notes of 250.0 US$m (February 2023), the 9.125% notes, 650.0 US$m outstanding at December 31, 2025 (indenture dated November 20, 2023), and the 8.875% notes of 550.0 US$m (indenture dated July 22, 2024) (10-K page:103 to page:104 and page:135). No new debt was issued in 2026 through the cutoff: the 7.50% senior guaranteed notes due January 2028 were redeemed on January 15, 2026, and 100.0 US$m of the 9.125% notes was redeemed for about 104.9 US$m in cash in the third quarter, taking notes at face value to 2,050.0 US$m (10-K page:103; 10-Q Q3 page:15; CP-1). On April 7, 2026 a joinder increased the credit agreement's letter of credit tranche by 25.0 US$m, and on September 4, 2025 the first amendment let Nabors Delaware repurchase up to 100.0 US$m of equity a year, reducing dividend capacity dollar for dollar (10-Q Q3 page:16). The special purpose acquisition company NETC II, co-sponsored with an entity owned by members of management and directors, failed to complete its planned combination with e2Companies; after litigation, a settlement on October 14, 2025 gave NETC II a secured promissory note from e2 of 29.23 US$m, and 10.6 US$m of settlement income was recorded in Other, net in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (10-Q Q3 page:30; 10-K page:113).

On August 26, 2026 Nabors issued about 0.4 million common shares for about 5.4 million Series B-1 preferred shares of Quaise Energy, Inc., a noncash exchange valued by reference to 35.0 US$m (10-Q Q3 page:17); this is an equity investment funded with shares, not cash or debt. As subsequent events after September 30, 2026 and before the cutoff, the October 27, 2026 release reports that SANAD deployed its 17th newbuild rig, that one more is scheduled for 2026 and two for the first quarter of 2027, that Nabors signed a multiyear contract to deploy one rig in Venezuela in early 2027, and that SANAD suspended five rigs (E14, E15, E16, E17). These are management statements in a furnished release; the filed 10-Q gives none of these counts. No sponsor, no dividend recapitalisation, no priming or uptier exchange and no debt-funded distribution appears in the pack. Nothing dated after the cutoff is used.

### Credit translations

**Revenue durability and concentration.** Evidence: Saudi Aramco about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues, the three largest customers about 41%, contracts per rig through SANAD (E4, E5, E22), and 2026 suspension and reactivation notices in the Middle East (E24, E32). Risk mechanic: per-rig contracts let a customer idle rigs without a contract termination, so a suspension reduces revenue, EBITDA and receivable inflows at once while SANAD's newbuild obligations and Nabors' backstop continue; 41% of receivables sit in Saudi Arabia. Credit implication: debt service capacity depends on one counterparty's rig program, so the monitoring posture should track SANAD rig count and receivables from Saudi Arabia each quarter; the Q3 2026 filed rig counts rose, but management reports five suspended rigs after quarter end. Countering logged item: conflict C3 (Aramco share versus related-party revenue) means the size of the concentration is not fully pinned down.

**Margin and cash-flow risk.** Evidence: daywork dayrate contracts, lower U.S. dayrates offset by volume, improving international pricing, and a management guide that includes a large SANAD newbuild program (E19, E23, E24, E27). Risk mechanic: margin depends on dayrate and rigs working, while SANAD capital spending is front-loaded and its timing has shifted to later periods. Credit implication: free cash flow after capital spending is sensitive to SANAD milestone timing, so the debt reduction already achieved came from cash balances rather than recurring surplus (CP-1).

**Ownership and sponsor alignment.** Evidence: no sponsor or controlling holder is identified; change of control may accelerate debt and trigger a call option on the SANAD interest (E30). Risk mechanic: a control event would hit funding and the asset base together. Credit implication: sponsor alignment cannot be assessed beyond documented actions; behaviour is Supportive on deleveraging and Neutral on related-party items, and the ownership gap is a monitoring item.

**Portfolio change.** Evidence: Parker acquired for shares and Quail Tools sold for cash within six months (E11, E12). Risk mechanic: FY2025 reported earnings include a business sold in August 2025 and a bargain purchase gain, so history overstates the continuing base. Credit implication: LTM figures from CP-1 are the cleaner base; the conflict on the sale price (C1) does not change the cash received of 375.0 US$m and the prepaid seller note of 250.0 US$m.
**Key uncertainties.** Backlog, SANAD earnings, guarantor structure and covenant definitions are not available (R8, CP-1 H2 and H3). Missing evidence is not an adverse conclusion.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Nabors has moderate leverage, no maturities before June 2029 and 825.1 US$m of liquidity, but earnings and receivables lean on Saudi Aramco and the SANAD venture. The credit view is balanced, with business risk the main weakness. | Medium | Cash interest for 2026, the covenant EBITDA definition, SANAD earnings and backlog are not available, and the October rig-suspension news is a management statement. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| About 30% of FY2025 revenue comes from Saudi Aramco, 41% of receivables are in Saudi Arabia, and management reports five suspended SANAD rigs. | One counterparty's rig program drives earnings, receivables and capital needs, so Saudi activity is the key monitoring item. | High |

| Net debt is 1.76x LTM adjusted EBITDA, notes at face value are 2,050.0 US$m, and the first maturity is in June 2029. | Leverage is moderate and near-term refinancing risk is low, but the gross debt reduction came from cash, not from surplus cash flow. | Medium |

| Liquidity fell to 825.1 US$m from 1,290.7 US$m, and 180.6 US$m of cash sits in the half-owned SANAD venture. | The parent-level cushion is smaller than the headline, which matters if the receivables facility is not renewed after April 1, 2027. | Medium |

| Free cash flow after net capital spending was 170.4 US$m LTM against annual note coupons of 156.8 US$m. | Fixed charges are covered with little spare cash, and the margin depends on the timing of SANAD capital spending. | Medium |

| No sponsor or creditor-adverse action is documented; related-party arrangements and unavailable ownership detail remain monitoring items. | Governance adds no identified risk, but it cannot be fully assessed without the proxy statement and the legal documents. | Medium |
### Credit view

The fundamental credit view of Nabors Industries Ltd as of 2026-11-05 is balanced, with financial risk moderate and business risk elevated, and the confidence is Medium because the evidence is complete enough to judge direction but several datapoints that would move the view are missing. On the financial side, notes at face value stand at 2,050.0 US$m, net debt is 1,574.9 US$m or 1.76x LTM adjusted EBITDA of 893.6 US$m, gross leverage is 2.29x, no note matures before the 250.0 US$m exchangeable notes in June 2029, the revolver is undrawn at 350.0 US$m, and the reported covenant interest coverage of 5.20x sits well above the 2.75x minimum. The weakening features are the use of cash to fund the deleveraging, which lowered liquidity from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m while net leverage stayed flat at 1.74x to 1.76x, and a free cash flow margin over fixed charges that is thin. On the business side, Saudi Aramco is about 30% of FY2025 operating revenues and the 50% partner in the consolidated SANAD venture, so revenue durability, receivables, a large newbuild capital program and a change-of-control call option all depend on one relationship; the filings show reactivations of Saudi rigs during 2026 and the October release reports five suspended SANAD rigs, which are management statements not yet in a filing. Governance evidence is neutral to supportive: debt has been repaid in cash, no sponsor or creditor-adverse action is documented, and the related-party arrangements are disclosed but only partly quantified. What would change the view: confirmed Saudi suspensions that cut earnings or collections, a non-renewal of the receivables facility, or evidence that SANAD cash and earnings are less accessible to creditors than the consolidated figures imply would weaken it; sustained free cash flow above fixed charges and further cash-funded debt reduction without eroding liquidity would strengthen it.

| Item | View | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Fundamental credit view | Balanced: moderate financial risk, elevated business risk from customer and joint venture concentration; no recovery outcome or relative value is stated | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1A: concentration, SANAD mechanics, governance behaviour, conflicts; CP-1: leverage, liquidity, maturity and covenant figures |

| Financial risk and liquidity | Moderate leverage, adequate liquidity with a smaller cushion than at FY2025, no near-term maturity | Documentary Fact | Medium | CP-1: Chart data leverage, liquidity and debt maturities; Financials and credit metrics |

| Business risk | Elevated by concentration in Saudi Aramco and SANAD, offset by diversified segments and technology revenue | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1A: customers, operating model, ownership rows |

| Limits on the view | Cash interest for 2026, covenant EBITDA, guarantor and ranking detail, SANAD earnings, backlog and beneficial ownership are not available | Insufficient Information | Not applicable | CP-0 and CP-1 gaps; CP-1A gaps |
### Credit thesis
| Thesis | Category | Basis |

| Nabors is a moderately levered, diversified drilling contractor with a clear maturity runway and sound reported covenant headroom whose credit quality is set mainly by the durability of its Saudi Aramco and SANAD relationship and by whether free cash flow keeps pace with fixed charges. | Analyst Interpretation | CP-1 leverage, liquidity, maturity and cash flow figures; CP-1A concentration and SANAD rows |
### Key findings

The most important finding is concentration: Saudi Aramco accounted for about 30% of FY2025 consolidated operating revenues, the three largest contract drilling customers for about 41%, and about 41% of net receivables at September 30, 2026 were in Saudi Arabia. Because Aramco contracts are per rig and mainly run through SANAD, a customer decision to idle rigs cuts revenue and earnings without any contract termination, and the October release reports five suspended SANAD rigs against a quarter in which rig counts rose. That statement is management's, and until a filing confirms it the size of the effect cannot be stated.

The second finding is that leverage is moderate and has fallen on a gross basis only. Notes at face value fell from 2,529.1 to 2,050.0 US$m, gross leverage from 2.77x to 2.29x, but net debt moved only from 1,588.4 to 1,574.9 US$m, because the redemptions of the 2028 notes and part of the 2030 notes were paid from cash that fell from 940.7 to 475.1 US$m. Liquidity of cash plus the undrawn revolver therefore fell from 1,290.7 to 825.1 US$m. Third, the maturity profile is long: nothing matures before 250.0 US$m in June 2029, followed by 550.0, 550.0 and 700.0 US$m in 2030, 2031 and 2032, and the revolver runs to the earlier of June 17, 2029 and a springing date tied to the exchangeable notes; this limits refinancing risk for several years but concentrates 1,800.0 US$m in 2030 to 2032.

Fourth, free cash flow after net capital expenditures was 170.4 US$m on an LTM basis, 38.6 US$m for nine months 2026 and 74.5 US$m in Q3 2026, against annual coupons of 156.8 US$m on the notes outstanding; management guides full-year adjusted free cash flow of 100 to 110 US$m with SANAD newbuild spending included, and says Q3 spending was below forecast because milestones shifted. Fifth, SANAD is consolidated in full: 180.6 US$m of cash and 100% of its EBITDA are in the consolidated figures although Saudi Aramco owns half, redeemable noncontrolling interest of 502.7 US$m ranks as mezzanine equity, and Nabors has a disclosed backstop for its share of the first 25 rig purchases. Sixth, FY2025 earnings include Quail Tools, sold in August 2025, so LTM adjusted EBITDA of 893.6 US$m, against 912.7 US$m for FY2025, is the cleaner base; seventh, no sponsor, dividend recapitalisation or creditor-adverse action is documented, though related-party arrangements and the ownership gap remain to be monitored. Last, 2026 cash interest and the covenant EBITDA definition are not available, so coverage rests on interest expense (4.99x) and the reported covenant ratio.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. Moderate leverage with a long runway: net leverage of 1.76x on face value, the first maturity in June 2029, and a revolver that is undrawn and matures no earlier than that date. Reported covenant headroom is wide, with interest coverage at 5.20x against 2.75x and minimum guarantor value at 99.8% against 90%, though the covenant definition is not available to test. Diversification across four segments and across the U.S. and international drilling, with technology and equipment segments that sell to third parties. A demonstrated willingness to repay debt in cash and to refinance ahead of maturity, shown by the 2025 refinancing and the 2026 redemptions. Adjusted EBITDA on an LTM basis is above 890 US$m with interest cover on interest expense of 4.99x and falling coupons.

Weaknesses. Concentration in Saudi Aramco and in SANAD, which supplies about 30% of revenue and carries a rig-purchase backstop, a call option on Nabors' interest on a change of control, and a redeemable noncontrolling interest. A smaller liquidity cushion of 825.1 US$m, of which 180.6 US$m is SANAD cash, and a receivables facility of 168.0 US$m sold whose term may end on April 1, 2027. Thin free cash flow cover of fixed charges and dependence on the timing of SANAD capital spending. Heavy dependence on issuer-defined adjusted EBITDA that excludes certain cash expenses and includes all of SANAD. Information gaps on guarantors, ranking, covenant definitions, backlog and ownership. History distorted by gains and disposals in FY2025.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| The four earlier handoffs trace to the seven filings: 62 of 62 checked figure groups matched, and every recalculation reproduced. Only minor defects were found; committee use stays draft until an independent reviewer signs off. | Medium | This review was done by the same analyst session that wrote the handoffs, so it is not independent; legal documents, ratings and covenant definitions could not be traced at all. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Figures in the financial handoff reproduce from the filings and from each other, including leverage, liquidity, coverage and free cash flow. | Leverage, liquidity and coverage figures can be relied on as issuer-reported or correctly calculated, on the stated bases. | High |

| Management statements, such as the five suspended Saudi rigs and the guidance, stay attributed throughout and are not presented as filed fact. | The Saudi downside is flagged but not sized; confirmation in a filing is needed before it is treated as established. | Medium |

| Five minor issues were found: an unsupported descriptor, an unextracted figure, a misplaced locator, an unexplained covenant ratio difference and the lack of reviewer independence. | None changes a credit conclusion or any ratio, but each needs the stated fix or acknowledgement. | High |

| Guarantor, ranking, security and covenant definition claims rest on filing summaries, not on the indentures or the credit agreement. | Structural priority and covenant headroom cannot be treated as verified until those documents are reviewed. | Medium |

### Evidence trace view

The evidence trace holds. Across the four handoffs, 62 groups of figures and locators were re-opened against the pinned filings and every group matched the page it cites, every derived figure in CP-1 and CP-2 was recomputed from its stated inputs and reproduced, the quotes in the evidence registers of CP-0, CP-1 and CP-1A are exact substrings of the cited pages, and the four modules agree on the same values for net debt, leverage, liquidity, coupons, free cash flow, customer concentration and the conflicts that were logged. The strongest supported contrary evidence to the cautious credit view in CP-2 is the Q3 2026 operating improvement in the filings, with higher rig counts, adjusted free cash flow of 74.5 US$m and reported covenant coverage of 5.20x; the handoffs take it into account, so it would win only if the October rig suspensions proved immaterial and SANAD spending stayed below plan. The weakest-supported element is the Saudi downside, because the five suspended rigs and the guidance are management statements in a furnished release that no filing repeats, and the handoffs correctly tag them as such. Five minor issues were found and are logged below; none is Critical or Material, so the severity engine gives a QA status of Passed, but committee use is Draft Only because the reviewer is not independent of the author, legal documents and ratings were never supplied, and the covenant EBITDA definition cannot be read. The risk mechanism for the unverified parts is direct: guarantor, ranking and covenant claims that rest on summaries could move structural priority and headroom conclusions if the executed documents differ, so those conclusions carry the label of summary evidence.
